title: SWE-smith for Multilingual Codebases: Scaling Software Engineering Training Data Beyond Python
description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates scalable training data generation for Python, but real-world software engineering spans diverse languages (TypeScript, Java, Rust, Go). Models trained only on Python data show poor transfer to other languages, limiting practical utility of autonomous coding agents. Proposed Method: We extend the SWE-smith pipeline to support multilingual codebase processing by (1) developing language-agnostic environment containerization using language-specific package managers (npm, Maven, Cargo, Go modules), (2) adapting the test-breaking synthesis procedure to leverage language-specific test frameworks (Jest, JUnit, cargo test, go test), and (3) designing a cross-lingual trajectory collection system that captures agent reasoning across language contexts. We additionally propose a multilingual mixture training strategy that balances instances across languages during fine-tuning, using language-weighted sampling to prevent Python dominance. Experiments: We construct datasets of ~10k instances each for TypeScript, Java, Rust, and Go from 30+ repositories per language. We evaluate trained models on SWE-bench Verified (Python), a newly constructed SWE-bench-TS benchmark derived from popular TypeScript repositories, and cross-lingual transfer benchmarks. We ablate mixture ratios and analyze whether multilingual training improves or degrades Python performance, measuring resolve rates and execution success across all languages.

title: SWE-Diverse: Improving Software Engineering Agent Generalization via Structured Difficulty-Aware Curriculum Learning on Synthetic Task Instances
description: Problem: While SWE-smith dramatically scales training data quantity, simply training on 50k instances uniformly may not optimally develop an agent's problem-solving capabilities. Instances vary enormously in difficulty (single-line fixes vs. multi-file refactors), and naive uniform sampling likely causes agents to overfit on easy patterns while underperforming on complex real-world bugs. Proposed Method: We introduce a curriculum learning framework specifically for software engineering agents. First, we define an automated difficulty scoring function using proxy signals: number of files changed, test complexity, edit distance of ground-truth patch, and static analysis metrics. Second, we cluster SWE-smith's 50k instances into difficulty tiers. Third, we train SWE-agent-LM with a structured curriculum—starting from easy instances and progressively introducing harder ones—while dynamically adjusting sampling probabilities based on per-tier validation performance. We also experiment with self-paced learning where the model's current failure rate on held-out tier samples governs curriculum progression. Experiments: We evaluate on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Lite, comparing (1) uniform training, (2) hard-instance-focused training, (3) proposed curriculum training, and (4) ablations of difficulty signals. We additionally analyze whether curriculum-trained models generalize better to unseen repositories not present in SWE-smith's 128-repo training set.

title: SWE-Diversity: Quality-Aware Curriculum Learning for Software Engineering Agents via Difficulty-Stratified Synthetic Data
description:
Problem: While SWE-smith dramatically scales training data volume, simply having 50k instances does not address whether training on all instances equally is optimal. Many synthetic bug instances may be trivially easy or pathologically hard, leading to inefficient learning. Curriculum learning—presenting training examples in a difficulty-ordered progression—has proven effective in other domains but remains unexplored for software engineering agents.

Method: We propose a quality-aware curriculum learning framework built on top of SWE-smith data. First, we automatically estimate instance difficulty using proxy signals: test complexity (number of assertions, cyclomatic complexity of failing tests), patch size, and pass-rate across a pool of weaker baseline models. We then partition the 50k dataset into difficulty tiers (easy/medium/hard) and train using three curriculum strategies: (1) easy-to-hard progression, (2) hard-to-easy, and (3) dynamic difficulty adjustment based on current model performance. We also introduce a diversity-aware sampling objective that maximizes coverage across repository types, error categories, and code domains to prevent overfitting to common patterns.

Experiments: We ablate curriculum strategies against uniform sampling baselines using SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Lite. We analyze learning curves, sample efficiency (performance vs. training examples seen), and generalization to held-out repositories not present in SWE-smith training data, demonstrating that data ordering and diversity matter as much as scale.

title: SWE-smith-Multi: Extending Automated Software Engineering Data Synthesis to Polyglot Repositories
description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates impressive scalability for Python codebases, but real-world software engineering increasingly involves polyglot repositories mixing JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, Go, and Rust. Models trained exclusively on Python data exhibit sharp performance drops on non-Python issues, limiting practical deployment. Proposed Method: We extend the SWE-smith pipeline to support four additional languages (JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, Go, Rust) by building language-specific execution environment constructors (leveraging Docker + language-native test runners like Jest, JUnit, go test, cargo test), and generalizing the fault-synthesis module to inject semantically diverse bugs using language-appropriate mutation operators (e.g., type coercions in TypeScript, null-pointer patterns in Java). We synthesize 10k+ task instances per language from 50+ repositories each, then train a unified polyglot SWE-agent by mixing data across languages with curriculum learning that gradually increases cross-language difficulty. Experiments: (1) Evaluate on SWE-bench Verified (Python) to confirm parity with baseline; (2) Construct SWE-bench-Poly, a new held-out benchmark of 500 real GitHub issues across the four target languages, measuring Pass@1 resolve rate; (3) Ablate mono-lingual vs. mixed training to quantify cross-language transfer; (4) Analyze failure modes by language and bug category to guide future data synthesis improvements.

title: SWE-smith-Multi: Extending Automated Software Engineering Data Synthesis to Polyglot Repositories
description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates impressive scaling for Python codebases, but real-world software engineering is polyglot—major systems mix JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, Go, Rust, and C++. Training data scarcity is even more acute for non-Python languages, leaving LM-based agents severely undertrained on large swaths of production code. Proposed Method: We extend the SWE-smith pipeline to support five additional languages (TypeScript, Java, Go, Rust, C++) by (1) building language-agnostic execution environment constructors using containerized build systems (Docker + language-specific package managers), (2) developing cross-language test-breaking mutation operators (type errors, API signature changes, logic mutations) adapted to each language's idioms and test frameworks (Jest, JUnit, go test, cargo test), and (3) training a router model that selects language-appropriate mutation strategies based on AST features. We generate 10k+ instances per language from 50+ GitHub repositories each, then fine-tune a 32B base model on the combined polyglot dataset using language-balanced sampling. Experiments: We evaluate on SWE-bench Verified (Python), a newly constructed SWE-bench-TS (TypeScript), and SWE-bench-Java benchmarks. Ablations study cross-language transfer—whether polyglot training improves Python performance—and per-language mutation strategy effectiveness, providing a comprehensive analysis of multilingual software engineering agent training.

title: SWE-smith-Multi: Extending Automated Software Engineering Data Synthesis to Multi-File, Cross-Module Bug Generation
description:
Problem: SWE-smith's synthesized bugs primarily target isolated test failures within single files or modules, but real-world software engineering issues frequently involve complex cross-module interactions, interface mismatches, and multi-file regressions. Models trained on single-file bugs may fail to generalize to these harder, more representative tasks.

Method: We extend the SWE-smith pipeline with a cross-module fault injection framework. Starting from dependency graphs of Python codebases, we identify inter-module API contracts (function signatures, return types, shared data structures). We then synthesize bugs by (1) introducing semantic interface mismatches across module boundaries, (2) injecting state corruption that propagates across call chains, and (3) mutating shared configuration/constants that affect multiple modules simultaneously. For each synthetic bug, we automatically identify the minimal set of files requiring edits to resolve it, creating labeled multi-file repair instances. We generate a 20k-instance dataset spanning 64 repositories.

Experiments: We fine-tune a 32B LM on multi-file instances and evaluate on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multifile (a new split we curate requiring ≥2 file edits), and SWELancer. We compare against SWE-agent-LM-32B trained on single-file data, measuring solve rate stratified by number of files modified, demonstrating that multi-file training data substantially improves performance on complex real-world issues without degrading single-file performance.

title: SWE-smith-Multi: Extending Scalable Software Engineering Data Synthesis to Multi-File, Cross-Module Bug Generation
description: Problem: SWE-smith generates task instances by breaking individual tests, which tends to produce localized, single-function bugs. Real-world software issues frequently involve cross-module interactions, API contract violations, or multi-file refactoring failures—precisely the harder class of bugs that distinguishes expert developers from novices, yet current training data underrepresents them. Method: We extend the SWE-smith pipeline with a cross-module bug synthesis module that (1) constructs a dependency graph of a repository's modules, (2) applies semantics-aware perturbations at interface boundaries (e.g., signature changes, altered return types, broken invariants propagated across call chains), and (3) uses an LM oracle to verify that the induced failure requires reasoning about multiple files before generating the task instance. We also introduce a difficulty-aware curriculum by clustering instances via call-graph depth and test-failure spread, enabling staged training. Experiments: We build a 20k-instance multi-file dataset from 50 large Python repositories. We fine-tune Qwen-2.5-32B with standard SWE-smith data, our multi-file data, and a curriculum mix, evaluating on SWE-bench Verified and a new SWE-bench-Hard split filtered to multi-file issues. We hypothesize the curriculum mix yields +3-5% on multi-file issues with no regression on single-file tasks.

title: SWE-Diversity: Quality-Aware Curriculum Learning for Software Engineering Agents via Difficulty-Stratified Synthetic Data
description:
Problem: While SWE-smith scales data quantity dramatically, not all 50k instances are equally informative for training. Naively mixing easy bug-fixes with complex multi-file refactoring tasks leads to suboptimal curriculum learning—models either plateau on easy examples or fail to generalize from hard ones. Current training procedures treat all instances uniformly, ignoring the pedagogical value of ordered exposure.

Proposed Method: We introduce a difficulty-aware curriculum learning framework for SWE training data. First, we design an automated difficulty scorer using static code metrics (cyclomatic complexity, edit distance, number of files changed, test coverage delta) combined with a lightweight proxy model's solve probability to assign difficulty tiers. Second, we apply curriculum learning strategies—baby-steps, competence-based, and self-paced—to order training instances. Third, we augment SWE-smith's pipeline to generate difficulty-balanced synthetic data by controlling the number and complexity of fault injection operations, ensuring diverse coverage across difficulty tiers.

Experiments: (1) Ablate curriculum ordering strategies vs. uniform sampling on SWE-bench Verified using SWE-agent-LM-32B. (2) Evaluate difficulty scorer correlation with actual agent success rates. (3) Compare difficulty-stratified subsets (10k, 25k) against full 50k uniform training. (4) Test cross-repository generalization to unseen repositories. We expect curriculum-trained models to improve 3-5% on hard SWE-bench instances while maintaining performance on easy ones.

title: SWE-smith for Multi-Language Codebases: Extending Automated Bug Synthesis Beyond Python to JavaScript, Java, and Rust
description: Problem: SWE-smith's pipeline is Python-specific, but real-world software engineering spans many languages. Models trained solely on Python data may fail to generalize to JavaScript, Java, or Rust ecosystems, leaving a significant gap in automated software engineering capabilities. Proposed Method: We extend SWE-smith's core pipeline—execution environment construction, test-breaking mutation synthesis, and trajectory collection—to three additional languages: JavaScript (Node.js/Jest), Java (Maven/Gradle/JUnit), and Rust (Cargo/test). Key challenges include adapting environment containerization for each ecosystem's package manager, designing language-appropriate mutation operators (e.g., type coercions for JS, ownership violations for Rust), and handling heterogeneous test frameworks. We produce a multilingual dataset of ~30k instances per language and fine-tune a single polyglot model (e.g., Qwen2.5-Coder-32B) jointly on all languages alongside the original Python data. Experiments: (1) Per-language resolve rate on newly constructed multilingual SWE-bench-style benchmarks, (2) Cross-language transfer analysis—does Python data help Rust performance and vice versa?, (3) Ablation on joint vs. language-specific fine-tuning, (4) Comparison against language-specialized baselines. Success would demonstrate that scalable bug synthesis generalizes across ecosystems, producing the first broadly multilingual SE agent training pipeline.

title: SWE-Diversity: Quality-Aware Curriculum Learning for Software Engineering Agents via Automated Difficulty Estimation
description: Problem: SWE-smith scales data quantity dramatically, but training on 50k instances uniformly ignores the difficulty distribution and semantic diversity of task instances. Easy or redundant instances may dilute training signal, while a naive mix can cause agents to overfit to common bug patterns from popular repositories. Proposed Method: We introduce SWE-Diversity, a curriculum learning framework that automatically estimates per-instance difficulty and semantic diversity to construct optimal training schedules. Difficulty is estimated using a lightweight proxy model (e.g., 7B LM) that predicts solve probability; diversity is measured via code-change embedding clustering across repository and bug-type dimensions. We then apply a three-stage curriculum: (1) warm-up on easy, high-diversity instances; (2) progressive introduction of hard instances weighted by coverage of underrepresented bug types; (3) fine-grained difficulty-adaptive sampling guided by live agent performance signals. Planned Experiments: (1) Ablate curriculum orderings (easy-to-hard, hard-to-easy, random, ours) on SWE-bench Verified using SWE-smith's 50k dataset; (2) Evaluate data efficiency—match SWE-agent-LM-32B's 40.2% using only 10k carefully selected instances; (3) Analyze which bug-type categories benefit most from curriculum ordering; (4) Test generalization to SWE-bench Multilingual to assess cross-language transfer under curriculum training.

title: SWE-Diversity: Curriculum-Guided Difficulty-Aware Sampling for Software Engineering Agent Training
description: Problem: SWE-smith generates 50k instances but treats them as a flat pool during training. Not all instances are equally informative — trivial bugs produce minimal learning signal while overly complex ones may confuse the model. There is no principled curriculum for ordering or weighting training instances by difficulty, diversity, or skill coverage. Method: We propose SWE-Diversity, a framework that (1) automatically estimates instance difficulty using proxy signals (number of failing tests, patch size, cyclomatic complexity of changed functions, edit distance from original code), (2) clusters instances by bug category (off-by-one, type errors, missing null checks, logic errors, etc.) using embedding-based clustering of problem descriptions and patches, and (3) applies curriculum learning with adaptive sampling — starting with easier, well-represented bug types and progressively introducing harder, rarer instances. We also introduce a diversity penalty to prevent over-fitting to frequent bug patterns. The curriculum schedule is learned via a bandit-style online algorithm that maximizes validation resolve rate improvement per training step. Experiments: We train 7B and 32B models on SWE-smith data with and without curriculum, measuring SWE-bench Verified resolve rate, training efficiency (performance vs. compute), and generalization to unseen repository types. We also ablate each curriculum component and analyze which bug categories benefit most from ordered training.

title: SWE-Diversity: Curriculum-Guided Difficulty-Aware Sampling for Software Engineering Agent Training
description: Problem: SWE-smith generates large volumes of training instances, but treats them as roughly equivalent during training. However, bug-fix tasks vary enormously in difficulty—some require single-line changes while others demand multi-file reasoning. Naively sampling uniformly from 50k instances may waste compute on trivial examples or overwhelm models with tasks far beyond their current capability, leaving the difficulty distribution's impact on agent performance unexplored. Proposed Method: We introduce a difficulty estimation module that scores each SWE-smith instance across three axes: (1) localization complexity (number of files/functions implicated), (2) test coverage density (how many tests fail and their structural diversity), and (3) edit distance of the ground-truth patch. Using these scores, we implement a curriculum learning strategy—training SWE-agent-LM models with progressively harder task batches using self-paced learning with automatic difficulty re-estimation after each epoch. We also apply diversity-aware sampling to ensure broad repository and bug-type coverage per batch. Experiments: We train 7B and 32B models on SWE-smith with (a) uniform sampling, (b) difficulty-ordered curriculum, (c) diversity-aware curriculum, and (d) combined strategy. We evaluate on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Lite, measuring Pass@1, training efficiency (resolve rate vs. compute), and generalization to held-out repositories not seen during training.

title: SWE-smith-Multi: Scaling Cross-Language Software Engineering Training Data via Language-Agnostic Test Breakage Synthesis
description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates powerful scalable data generation for Python, but real-world software engineering spans many languages (JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, Rust, Go). We introduce a unified task-instance schema that normalizes across languages and a cross-language curriculum training strategy that interleaves instances by difficulty and language. We train a single 32B model on 150k instances (50k per language group plus Python) using this curriculum. Planned Experiments: (1) Evaluate on SWE-bench Verified (Python) to confirm retention; (2) construct held-out multilingual benchmarks from 20+ repositories per language mirroring SWE-bench methodology; (3) ablate curriculum ordering vs. uniform sampling; (4) measure zero-shot transfer—does multilingual training improve Python performance? (5) compare against language-specific fine-tuned specialists. Expected outcome: a single open-source polyglot SWE agent surpassing per-language baselines through shared reasoning transfer.

title: SWE-smith-Multi: Extending Scalable Software Engineering Data Generation to Polyglot Repositories
description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrated scalable training data generation for Python repositories, but real-world software engineering increasingly involves polyglot codebases (TypeScript, Rust, Go, Java). We generate 20k+ task instances each for TypeScript, Rust, Go, and Java from 50+ repositories each, and train a unified polyglot SWE-agent on the combined dataset. Ablations examine cross-language transfer, data mixing ratios, and whether polyglot training helps or hurts Python performance compared to SWE-smith baselines.

title: SWE-smith-Multi: Cross-Language Scaling of Software Engineering Training Data Beyond Python
description:

Proposed Method: We extend SWE-smith's pipeline to support four additional languages by: (1) building language-specific execution environment constructors (npm/Maven/Cargo/Go modules), (2) designing AST-based fault injection operators adapted to each language's semantics (e.g., type-aware mutations for Rust/Java), (3) introducing a cross-language curriculum training strategy that progressively mixes language-specific data, and (4) creating a unified task representation schema enabling joint training across languages.

title: SWE-Diversity: Curriculum-Guided Difficulty Stratification for Software Engineering Training Data
description: Problem: SWE-smith generates large-scale training data but treats all 50k instances uniformly during training, ignoring the structural difficulty heterogeneity across task instances. Models trained on undifferentiated data may overfit to easy bug patterns while underperforming on complex, multi-file issues that appear in real benchmarks. Using these signals, we construct a curriculum learning schedule where training progresses from simple single-file fixes to complex multi-component repairs. We additionally propose a stratified data mixing strategy that maintains diversity across repositories and difficulty tiers per training batch. Experiments: We train 7B and 32B models on the full SWE-smith dataset under (a) uniform sampling, (b) difficulty-sorted curriculum, and (c) stratified mixing, evaluating on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Lite, and a held-out set of 'hard' instances filtered by human annotators. We ablate each difficulty axis to identify which factors most predict benchmark resolution rate, providing actionable data curation guidelines for future SE agent research.

title: SWE-Diversity: Curriculum-Guided Data Synthesis for Software Engineering Agents via Difficulty-Aware Instance Selection
description:

We further augment SWE-smith's synthesis with adversarial perturbations that generate 'near-miss' instances requiring subtle multi-hop reasoning.

title: SWE-Diversity: Curriculum-Guided Difficulty-Aware Training Data Synthesis for Software Engineering Agents
description: Problem: While SWE-smith scales the quantity of software engineering training instances, it treats all 50k instances uniformly during training. Research shows that curriculum learning—ordering training examples by difficulty—significantly improves agent performance, yet no principled difficulty estimation framework exists for SWE-bench-style tasks. Proposed Method: We introduce SWE-Diversity, a pipeline that augments SWE-smith-generated instances with automated difficulty scoring and curriculum scheduling. We estimate difficulty along three axes: (1) structural complexity (number of files/functions modified, cyclomatic complexity of affected code), (2) semantic distance (embedding similarity between bug description and relevant code), and (3) empirical hardness (pass rate across a small ensemble of weaker LM agents used as difficulty oracles). These scores feed a competence-based curriculum scheduler that progressively exposes the training agent to harder instances. Additionally, we use difficulty metadata to synthesize contrastive pairs—similar bugs at different difficulty levels—enabling difficulty-conditioned training. Experiments: We train 7B and 32B models on SWE-smith data with and without curriculum scheduling, evaluating on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Lite. Ablations isolate each difficulty axis's contribution. We also measure data efficiency: how many instances are needed with vs. without curriculum to reach a target resolve rate, demonstrating that smarter data ordering reduces compute requirements by 30-40%.

title: SWE-Diversity: Curriculum-Guided Difficulty-Aware Sampling for Software Engineering Agent Training
description:

We then apply three curriculum strategies: (1) easy-to-hard progressive training, (2) self-paced learning that dynamically re-weights instances based on current model solve rates, and (3) contrastive difficulty sampling that ensures mini-batches span the full difficulty spectrum. Experiments: Using SWE-smith's 50k dataset, we train variants of SWE-agent-LM-32B under each curriculum strategy, evaluating on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Lite. We analyze whether curriculum ordering improves sample efficiency (matching baseline performance with 50% of data), difficulty calibration quality, and generalization to held-out repositories not seen during training.

title: SWE-Diversity: Curriculum-Guided Difficulty Stratification for Software Engineering Training Data

Using these scores, we construct a curriculum training schedule that progresses from easy to hard instances, with an adaptive reweighting mechanism that dynamically adjusts sampling probabilities based on the current model's per-difficulty-tier success rate.

We analyze performance gains per difficulty tier, training efficiency (FLOPs to target accuracy), and out-of-distribution generalization to new repositories not seen during training.

Proposed Method: We extend SWE-smith's pipeline to support multi-language repository processing through three contributions: (1) a language-agnostic execution environment templating system using Docker and language-specific test harnesses (Jest, JUnit, Cargo test, Go test), (2) a universal test-breaking mutation strategy that operates at the AST level across languages using tree-sitter, applying semantics-preserving-but-behavior-altering transformations, and (3) a cross-lingual curriculum training procedure that progressively introduces task instances ordered by language similarity to Python, leveraging transfer learning. We generate a 30k-instance dataset spanning 5 languages from 200+ GitHub repositories. Experiments: We evaluate resulting models on SWE-bench Verified (Python), a new SWE-bench-JS benchmark we construct from 50 TypeScript repositories, and existing Java/Rust repair benchmarks. We measure cross-language transfer, compare curriculum vs. uniform mixing strategies, and ablate the contribution of each language to overall performance, demonstrating that multilingual SWE training substantially improves generalization without sacrificing Python performance.

title: SWE-Diversity: Curriculum-Guided Difficulty-Aware Sampling for Software Engineering Training Data
description: Problem: SWE-smith generates large quantities of training instances but treats them as a flat pool, ignoring the varying difficulty, diversity, and pedagogical ordering of instances. Training on uniform random samples from such data likely wastes compute on trivial instances or overwhelms models with tasks beyond their current capability, limiting sample efficiency. Method: We introduce SWE-Diversity, a framework that (1) automatically estimates instance difficulty using proxy signals—patch size, number of failing tests, cyclomatic complexity of modified functions, and zero-shot model solve rate—then (2) clusters instances by bug type (logic errors, missing branches, off-by-one, API misuse) using AST-diff embeddings to measure semantic diversity, and (3) applies curriculum learning with difficulty-aware sampling schedules that progress from easy to hard while maximizing inter-batch diversity via determinantal point process selection. Experiments: Using SWE-smith's 50k instance dataset, we train 7B and 32B base models under (a) uniform sampling, (b) difficulty-only curriculum, (c) diversity-only sampling, and (d) our joint curriculum+diversity approach. We evaluate on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Lite, measuring Pass@1 at multiple training compute checkpoints. We hypothesize our method achieves equivalent benchmark performance with 40-60% fewer training instances, improving data efficiency and providing insight into what makes software engineering training data valuable.

title: SWE-Critic: Learning a Reward Model for Software Engineering Agent Feedback via Synthetic Execution Traces
description: Problem: While SWE-smith provides abundant supervised training data for software engineering agents, the agents still rely on outcome-based binary signals (tests pass/fail) for reinforcement learning. This makes dense, step-level feedback during trajectory generation scarce, limiting sample efficiency and policy improvement. Proposed Method: We use SWE-smith's 50k task instances and their corresponding solution trajectories to train a dense reward model (SWE-Critic) that predicts, at each intermediate agent action (file edit, bash command, search query), how likely the current partial trajectory is to eventually resolve the issue. Specifically, we: (1) mine both successful and failed trajectories from SWE-smith, (2) label each action step with a discounted future success signal, (3) fine-tune a code-aware LM as a process reward model (PRM) using these labeled steps, and (4) integrate SWE-Critic into RLHF/GRPO training loops as a dense shaping signal. Experiments: We evaluate on SWE-bench Verified comparing (a) binary outcome RL baseline, (b) SWE-Critic-shaped RL, and (c) SWE-Critic used for best-of-N trajectory selection. We measure resolve rate, trajectory efficiency (steps to resolution), and generalization to repositories unseen during critic training, demonstrating that dense process supervision substantially improves agent performance beyond what outcome rewards alone provide.

title: SWE-Diversity: Quality-Aware Curriculum Sampling for Software Engineering Training Data
description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates that scale matters for SE training data, but scaling quantity alone may introduce redundant or low-quality instances that harm sample efficiency. When training on 50k instances from 128 repositories, the distribution of bug types, fix complexity, and code patterns is likely highly skewed, potentially causing models to overfit to common patterns while underperforming on rare but important bug categories. Proposed Method: We introduce a quality-aware curriculum sampling framework that operates on top of SWE-smith-generated data. First, we embed all task instances using a code-aware representation (e.g., AST-based features + LM embeddings) and apply diversity-maximizing selection via determinantal point processes to identify a core diverse subset. Second, we train a lightweight 'difficulty predictor' that estimates instance hardness from static code features, enabling curriculum learning that progressively introduces harder instances. Third, we apply cross-repository deduplication at the semantic level to remove near-duplicate bug patterns. Experiments: (1) Compare models trained on 10k/25k/50k instances selected via our method vs. random sampling on SWE-bench Verified; (2) Analyze per-category performance across bug types; (3) Ablate each component (diversity, curriculum, deduplication); (4) Measure training compute vs. performance tradeoffs. We hypothesize that 20k quality-selected instances match or exceed 50k randomly sampled instances.

title: SWE-Diversity: Quality-Aware Curriculum Sampling for Software Engineering Training Data
description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates that scaling to 50k instances dramatically improves agent performance, but raw scale alone may not be optimal — the distribution, difficulty, and diversity of training instances critically shape what agents learn. Current pipelines treat all generated instances equally, potentially over-representing easy bug patterns from popular repositories while underrepresenting challenging multi-file reasoning tasks. Method: We propose a quality-aware curriculum sampling framework that (1) automatically characterizes each SWE-smith instance along axes of difficulty (patch complexity, test coverage, file span), semantic diversity (AST-based clustering of bug types), and repository domain; (2) trains a lightweight 'difficulty predictor' from agent solve rates to score new instances without full rollouts; (3) applies curriculum learning — progressively sampling harder, more diverse instances throughout training — combined with coverage-based deduplication to reduce redundancy. We additionally introduce a 'cross-repository transfer score' to prioritize instances whose bug patterns generalize across codebases. Experiments: Using the SWE-smith pipeline and SWE-bench Verified as evaluation, we compare uniform sampling vs. difficulty-stratified vs. curriculum sampling at 10k/25k/50k instance budgets. We measure resolve rate, sample efficiency (performance per training instance), and generalization to unseen repositories, expecting curriculum sampling to match 50k uniform performance with 20k instances.

title: SWE-Diversity: Quality-Aware Filtering and Difficulty Stratification for Software Engineering Training Data
description:
Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates that scale matters for software engineering agents, but scaling data quantity alone may introduce redundancy, trivial instances, and uneven difficulty distributions that limit learning efficiency. Simply having 50k instances does not guarantee they collectively maximize model capability across diverse bug types and reasoning depths.

Proposed Method: We introduce SWE-Diversity, a post-hoc dataset curation framework that operates on top of SWE-smith-style pipelines. First, we embed task instances using code-aware embeddings (e.g., CodeBERT or StarCoder embeddings) and apply coverage-maximizing selection (facility location submodular optimization) to reduce redundancy while preserving diversity across bug categories, repository domains, and fix complexity. Second, we train a lightweight difficulty estimator that predicts instance solve-rate from static features (edit distance, number of files changed, test complexity), enabling curriculum learning schedules that progress from easier to harder instances. Third, we incorporate a quality filter that discards instances where the synthetic bug is trivially detectable via linting or type-checking alone.

Experiments: (1) Train SWE-agent models on filtered subsets of 5k/10k/25k instances vs. random equivalents, measuring SWE-bench Verified Pass@1. (2) Ablate each filtering component independently. (3) Compare curriculum vs. random ordering using the same filtered dataset. (4) Analyze whether difficulty-stratified training improves performance on hard SWE-bench instances specifically, using the recently released SWE-bench difficulty tiers.

title: SWE-polyglot: Extending Scalable Software Engineering Data Generation Beyond Python to Multi-Language Codebases
description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates scalable task generation but is restricted to Python repositories, leaving vast ecosystems (JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, Go, Rust) underserved. Real-world software engineering agents must handle polyglot codebases, yet no large-scale multi-language training dataset exists. Method: We extend SWE-smith's pipeline to support four additional languages by (1) developing language-agnostic execution environment constructors using containerized build systems (npm, Maven, Cargo, Go modules), (2) creating language-specific fault injection strategies that exploit type systems, async patterns, and idiomatic constructs beyond Python's dynamic features, and (3) implementing cross-language trajectory collection by adapting SWE-agent's tool use (file editing, test execution, linting) for each language's toolchain. We generate ~10k instances per language (40k total) from 50+ repositories each, yielding a 200k+ instance polyglot dataset. Experiments: (1) Train language-specific and unified polyglot models based on Qwen-2.5-32B, evaluating on SWE-bench Verified (Python), plus newly constructed held-out benchmarks for each language following SWE-bench's methodology. (2) Measure cross-language transfer: does training on polyglot data improve Python performance and vice versa? (3) Ablate fault injection strategies per language to identify which techniques generalize. Target: establish first open-source multi-language SWE benchmark and baseline models.

title: SWE-Diversity: Quality-Aware Curriculum Sampling for Software Engineering Training Data
description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates that scale matters for software engineering agents, but simply having 50k instances does not guarantee diverse, balanced, or appropriately difficult training data. Models trained on large but redundant or skewed datasets may overfit to common bug patterns from popular repositories while failing on rare-but-important bug categories. Method: We propose a quality-aware curriculum sampling framework that operates on top of SWE-smith-style datasets. First, we embed all task instances using code-aware representations (e.g., AST-based features, test complexity metrics, repository domain tags) and apply diversity-maximizing clustering to identify underrepresented bug categories. Second, we train a difficulty estimator (using proxy metrics like number of files changed, test depth, cyclomatic complexity) to enable curriculum learning—ordering training from easy to hard. Third, we introduce a deduplication filter based on semantic similarity of generated patches to remove near-duplicate instances. Experiments: (1) Train SWE-agent variants with random sampling vs. our curriculum on SWE-bench Verified, measuring Pass@1 and sample efficiency. (2) Ablate each component (diversity sampling, curriculum ordering, deduplication) independently. (3) Evaluate cross-repository generalization on held-out repositories not seen during training. (4) Analyze whether models trained with diversity-aware sampling better handle rare bug types (concurrency, memory, algorithmic errors).

title: SWE-Diversity: Quality-Aware Curriculum Sampling for Software Engineering Training Data
description:
Problem: SWE-smith scales data quantity dramatically (50k instances), but training on all instances uniformly may be suboptimal—many synthesized bug instances may be trivially easy, redundant, or misleadingly noisy, potentially diluting learning signal from genuinely challenging and diverse examples. Naive scaling assumes more data is always better, ignoring data quality and curriculum effects.

Proposed Method: We introduce a quality-aware curriculum sampling framework for SWE-smith data. First, we characterize each task instance along multiple dimensions: (1) solution complexity (patch size, AST edit distance), (2) test coverage diversity (which code paths are exercised), (3) repository origin clustering (avoiding repository-level redundancy), and (4) model-estimated difficulty (probability assigned by a small reference model). We then train with a dynamic curriculum that progressively samples harder, more diverse instances using a multi-armed bandit scheduler that balances exploration of difficulty tiers against exploitation of high-learning-signal instances. We further apply automated quality filtering to remove near-duplicate instances via code embedding similarity.

Experiments: (1) Ablate curriculum strategies (random, difficulty-sorted, bandit) on SWE-bench Verified using 5k/15k/50k data budgets; (2) Compare uniform 50k training vs. curated 10k subset; (3) Analyze whether quality filtering changes repository-level performance distribution; (4) Test transfer to SWE-bench Multilingual with Python-trained curricula.

title: SWE-Diversity: Quality-Aware Curriculum Learning for Software Engineering Agents via Difficulty-Stratified Training Data
description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates that scaling training data volume dramatically improves software engineering agent performance, but naively scaling to 50k instances treats all examples equally, ignoring that task difficulty varies enormously across repositories and bug types. Training on undifferentiated data may cause models to overfit easy patterns while underlearning complex multi-file refactoring or subtle logic errors. Proposed Method: We introduce SWE-Diversity, a framework that automatically characterizes and stratifies SWE-smith-style task instances by difficulty dimensions (patch size, number of files modified, test complexity, error type taxonomy, cyclomatic complexity of affected code). We then implement a curriculum learning strategy that progressively exposes the model to harder instances, combined with a difficulty-aware data mixing policy that upsamples underrepresented hard instances. We additionally propose a quality filter using execution-verified 'golden trajectory' consistency scoring—retaining only trajectories where multiple independent agent rollouts converge on the same solution. Experiments: We train models on SWE-bench Verified using (1) flat SWE-smith baseline, (2) curriculum ordering, (3) quality filtering alone, and (4) combined approach. We evaluate Pass@1, Pass@5, and performance broken down by difficulty tier. We hypothesize that difficulty-stratified training with quality filtering achieves comparable or better performance using 30-40% fewer training instances, improving data efficiency substantially.

title: SWE-Diversity: Automated Difficulty-Stratified Data Synthesis for Curriculum Learning in Software Engineering Agents
description: Problem: SWE-smith generates large-scale training data but treats all instances uniformly during training, ignoring the varying complexity of bug-fix tasks. Training on undifferentiated data may lead to suboptimal learning dynamics—easy tasks dominate gradient updates while hard tasks are underutilized. Proposed Method: We introduce SWE-Diversity, a pipeline that automatically characterizes instance difficulty across multiple axes (cyclomatic complexity, number of files touched, test dependency depth, edit distance of gold patch) and constructs a difficulty-stratified curriculum for training software engineering agents. We augment SWE-smith's generation pipeline with a lightweight difficulty oracle (trained on static code features + LM-based solvability probes) to label each instance. We then apply curriculum learning strategies—baby-step, self-paced, and competence-based scheduling—during fine-tuning of base LMs on the 50k SWE-smith instances. Planned Experiments: (1) Evaluate multiple curriculum schedules vs. uniform training on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Lite using 7B and 32B models; (2) Ablate difficulty dimensions to identify which features best predict instance utility for training; (3) Analyze where resolved issues cluster on the difficulty spectrum post-curriculum; (4) Test generalization to new repositories unseen during training. We expect curriculum-trained models to achieve 3-5% absolute improvement over uniform baselines with identical data.

title: SWE-smith for Multi-Language Repositories: Extending Automated Bug Synthesis Beyond Python
description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates scalable training data generation for Python codebases, but real-world software engineering increasingly involves polyglot repositories (TypeScript, Java, Rust, Go). Agents trained purely on Python data underperform on non-Python tasks, yet no comparable large-scale training datasets exist for other languages. Proposed Method: We extend SWE-smith's pipeline to support TypeScript/JavaScript, Java, and Rust by (1) building language-specific execution environment constructors using Docker with appropriate runtime toolchains, (2) adapting the bug synthesis strategies—mutation operators tailored to each language's idioms (e.g., type annotation stripping for TypeScript, lifetime violations for Rust), and (3) designing unified fault-localization and test-failure verification harnesses that work across language runtimes. We synthesize ~10k instances per language from 30+ popular GitHub repositories each, producing a 40k-instance multi-language benchmark. Planned Experiments: (1) Train SWE-agent-LM variants on single-language vs. mixed-language data to measure cross-language transfer. (2) Evaluate on existing benchmarks: SWE-bench Verified (Python), GitBug-Java, and a newly constructed TypeScript-bench derived from top npm packages. (3) Ablate mutation strategy diversity and test-suite density to identify what drives data quality across languages. Target outcome: a publicly released multi-language training corpus and strong open-source baseline agents across four languages.

title: SWE-Diverse: Multilingual Software Engineering Training Data via Cross-Language Bug Synthesis
description:
Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates scalable training data generation for Python, but real-world software engineering spans many languages (JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, Rust, Go, C++). Current benchmarks and training pipelines are almost exclusively Python-centric, leaving LM agents poorly calibrated for multilingual codebases that dominate industry settings.

Proposed Method: We extend the SWE-smith pipeline to support non-Python repositories by (1) building language-specific execution environment constructors that handle polyglot package managers (npm, cargo, gradle, maven) and test runners (jest, cargo test, junit, pytest), (2) designing a universal bug-synthesis module that mutates AST nodes using language-specific grammar rules via tree-sitter, breaking existing test suites analogously to SWE-smith's Python approach, and (3) training a single multilingual SWE-agent using combined cross-language trajectories with a language-routing prefix token.

Planned Experiments: (1) Construct datasets of ~5k instances each for JS/TS, Java, Rust, and Go from 20+ popular GitHub repositories per language. (2) Train multilingual SWE-agent-LM variants (7B, 32B) on combined data. (3) Evaluate on SWE-bench Verified (Python) and newly constructed SWE-bench-ML (multilingual held-out benchmark with 300 verified instances per language). (4) Ablate cross-language transfer: does joint training help or hurt per-language performance vs. language-specific models?

title: SWE-Diversity: Quality-Aware Data Selection for Software Engineering Agents via Difficulty-Stratified Curriculum Learning
description: Problem: While SWE-smith scales dataset size to 50k instances, simply training on all generated data treats easy and hard bug-fixing tasks uniformly. This ignores the well-established observation that curriculum learning—presenting training examples in a meaningful difficulty progression—can significantly improve sample efficiency and final performance of LMs. Proposed Method: We introduce SWE-Diversity, a difficulty-aware data selection and curriculum learning framework built on top of SWE-smith. First, we estimate instance difficulty using proxy signals: (1) number of files/functions modified in the ground-truth patch, (2) test coverage complexity of the broken tests, (3) semantic distance between bug description and relevant code, and (4) a small 7B model's Pass@k on a held-out subset. Using these signals, we construct a multi-dimensional difficulty score and design three training curricula: easy-to-hard, hard-to-easy, and competence-based adaptive scheduling. We additionally apply quality filtering to remove near-duplicate or trivially-solved instances. Experiments: We train 7B and 32B models on SWE-smith data under each curriculum and compare against uniform random sampling baselines. Evaluation is on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Lite, and a held-out set of 500 instances from novel repositories. We report Pass@1 resolve rate, training efficiency (performance vs. number of gradient steps), and generalization to out-of-distribution repositories.

title: SWE-smith for Multilingual Codebases: Scaling Software Engineering Training Data Beyond Python
description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates scalable task generation for Python, but real-world software engineering spans multiple languages (TypeScript, Java, Rust, Go). Models trained only on Python SWE tasks show poor cross-language generalization, limiting their utility for enterprise codebases that are predominantly non-Python. Proposed Method: We extend the SWE-smith pipeline to support TypeScript, Java, and Rust by (1) developing language-specific execution environment constructors leveraging Docker with language-appropriate build systems (npm/jest, Maven/JUnit, cargo/test), (2) designing language-agnostic fault injection strategies that break existing tests through AST-level mutations adapted per language semantics (e.g., type errors for TypeScript, null pointer patterns for Java, borrow-checker boundary cases for Rust), and (3) curating 10k+ task instances per language from 50+ GitHub repositories each. We then train multilingual SWE-agents using a joint training regime combining Python SWE-smith data with our new multilingual instances. Experiments: We evaluate on SWE-bench Verified (Python), and construct new multilingual benchmarks from held-out repositories for each target language, measuring Pass@1 resolve rates. We further analyze cross-language transfer: does training on multilingual data improve Python performance and vice versa? Ablations study per-language data volume and fault injection strategy effectiveness.

title: SWE-Diversity: Curriculum-Guided Difficulty-Aware Sampling for Software Engineering Agent Training
description: Problem: While SWE-smith dramatically scales the quantity of training instances, all 50k instances are treated uniformly during training despite substantial variation in task difficulty, code complexity, and bug type diversity. This likely leads to inefficient learning—easy instances waste compute while very hard instances may confuse the model early in training. Proposed Method: We introduce SWE-Diversity, a curriculum learning framework built atop SWE-smith data. First, we automatically characterize each instance across multiple axes: (1) difficulty signals (number of failing tests, patch size, cyclomatic complexity of changed code), (2) bug category (logic errors, type errors, missing edge cases, API misuse) via lightweight LM classification, and (3) repository domain (web, scientific computing, CLI tools). We then train with a dynamic curriculum scheduler that progressively introduces harder instances, combined with diversity-aware batch sampling that enforces coverage across bug categories and domains in each batch. We also apply instance reweighting based on per-instance training loss trajectories to deprioritize 'mastered' examples. Experiments: We train multiple 32B variants on SWE-smith data with different curricula and compare on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Lite, and a held-out repository split measuring generalization. We ablate each curriculum component and analyze whether difficulty-stratified training yields better sample efficiency and cross-repository generalization than uniform sampling.

title: SWE-Diversity: Quality-Aware Curriculum Sampling for Software Engineering Training Data
description: Problem: While SWE-smith dramatically scales training data quantity (50k instances), naively training on all instances may be suboptimal — many synthesized bugs may cluster around simple, repetitive patterns (e.g., off-by-one errors, trivial assertion changes), leaving agents undertrained on complex, multi-file reasoning tasks that dominate real-world software engineering. Method: We propose a quality-aware curriculum learning framework that automatically characterizes difficulty and diversity of SWE-smith instances along axes including: (1) patch complexity (lines changed, files touched, cyclomatic complexity delta), (2) semantic novelty via embedding-based clustering of bug descriptions and patches, (3) test coverage impact, and (4) agent solve-rate from lightweight proxy models. We then train agents using curriculum schedules that progressively introduce harder and more diverse instances, combined with active data selection that upsamples underrepresented difficulty strata. We additionally apply deduplication and quality filtering to remove near-duplicate instances. Experiments: We evaluate on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Lite, comparing uniform sampling vs. curriculum strategies using the SWE-agent-LM-32B backbone. Ablations isolate each difficulty axis. We hypothesize that training on 15k carefully selected instances outperforms training on the full 50k, demonstrating that data quality and curriculum design matter as much as scale.

title: SWE-smith for Low-Resource Languages: Extending Automated Bug Synthesis Beyond Python to Multilingual Codebases
description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates scalable bug synthesis for Python, but the vast majority of real-world software engineering occurs in non-Python languages (Java, TypeScript, Go, Rust, C++). Language models trained exclusively on Python-derived tasks show degraded performance on these languages, yet no comparable large-scale training datasets exist for them. Proposed Method: We extend the SWE-smith pipeline to support Java, TypeScript, and Go by (1) building language-agnostic execution environment constructors using containerized build systems (Maven/Gradle, npm/tsc, go build), (2) adapting the fault injection strategies—mutation operators, test-breaking perturbations—to language-specific AST structures using tree-sitter, and (3) developing a cross-lingual trajectory synthesis module that generates agent solution traces in each target language. We additionally propose a multilingual curriculum training strategy where a base model is progressively fine-tuned starting from Python (data-rich) toward lower-resource languages, with cross-lingual transfer signals. Experiments: We construct datasets of 10k+ instances per language from popular GitHub repositories, train language-specific and multilingual SWE agents, and evaluate on SWE-bench equivalents for each language (GitBug-Java, TypeScript-bench). We measure resolve rate, data efficiency curves, and cross-language transfer gains versus language-specific baselines, targeting a 15%+ improvement over zero-shot GPT-4o on non-Python benchmarks.

title: SWE-smith for Multilingual Codebases: Scaling Software Engineering Training Data Beyond Python
description: Problem: SWE-smith's pipeline is Python-specific, yet real-world software engineering increasingly involves polyglot codebases (TypeScript, Rust, Java, Go). Current benchmarks and training data for non-Python languages are virtually nonexistent, leaving LMs poorly equipped for cross-language bug fixing. Proposed Method: We extend SWE-smith's core pipeline to support TypeScript, Java, and Rust by (1) building language-specific execution environment constructors using Docker with appropriate build toolchains (npm/Jest, Maven/JUnit, Cargo), (2) adapting the fault-injection synthesis module to leverage language-specific AST parsers (tree-sitter) for generating test-breaking mutations (type errors, logic inversions, API misuse), and (3) creating a unified task-instance schema that normalizes across languages while preserving language-specific context. We generate ~10k instances per language from 30+ GitHub repositories each. Experiments: We fine-tune CodeLlama-34B and Qwen2.5-Coder-32B on language-specific and mixed-language datasets, evaluating on newly constructed SWE-bench-TS, SWE-bench-Java, and SWE-bench-Rust held-out benchmarks. We measure cross-language transfer (train on Python, test on TypeScript) and polyglot joint training benefits. Ablations examine whether language-agnostic vs. language-specific fault injection strategies affect data quality and downstream resolve rates.

title: SWE-Diversity: Quality-Aware Difficulty Stratification and Curriculum Learning for Software Engineering Agents
description: Problem: SWE-smith scales data volume dramatically, but 50k instances sourced uniformly may contain redundant, trivial, or misleading training signals. Training on flat distributions of task instances ignores the pedagogical insight that curriculum ordering—easy-to-hard progression—can significantly improve agent learning efficiency and final performance. Method: We propose SWE-Diversity, a framework that augments SWE-smith's pipeline with (1) an automatic difficulty estimator using static code complexity metrics (cyclomatic complexity, dependency depth, test coverage delta) combined with a small proxy LM's pass/fail predictions to assign difficulty scores to each instance; (2) a semantic deduplication module using AST-based code embeddings to cluster and prune near-duplicate bug patterns; and (3) a curriculum training scheduler that presents instances in adaptive difficulty order, with dynamic reweighting based on the current model's evolving performance profile. We also introduce a diversity reward during data synthesis to explicitly encourage varied bug types (logic errors, boundary conditions, concurrency issues). Experiments: We compare flat vs. curriculum training on SWE-bench Verified using 32B models trained on 10k/25k/50k subsets drawn by our stratification vs. random sampling. We measure final resolve rate, training efficiency (steps to 30% resolve), and generalization to held-out repositories. We expect curriculum ordering yields equivalent performance with 40% less training data.

title: SWE-smith-Multi: Scaling Cross-Language Software Engineering Training Data Beyond Python
description:
Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates impressive scalability for Python repositories, but real-world software engineering spans dozens of languages (JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, Go, Rust, C++). Models trained exclusively on Python data exhibit poor cross-language transfer, limiting their utility for the majority of production codebases. Existing non-Python SWE benchmarks remain tiny (<500 instances), starving research in multilingual automated software engineering.

Proposed Method: We extend the SWE-smith pipeline to support JavaScript/TypeScript (Jest/Mocha), Java (JUnit/Maven), and Go (go test) ecosystems. Key technical contributions include: (1) language-agnostic execution environment containerization using a unified Dockerfile templating system, (2) AST-based fault injection operators tailored per language (e.g., type annotation removal for TypeScript, interface mutation for Go), (3) cross-language instance filtering using test flakiness detection adapted for each test framework, and (4) a unified data schema enabling mixed-language training.

Experiments: We generate 30k+ instances per language from 50+ repositories each. We train a multilingual SWE-agent on combined data and evaluate on: (1) SWE-bench Verified (Python), (2) a newly constructed JS-bench and Java-bench of 300 instances each, and (3) cross-language zero-shot transfer experiments. We ablate single-language vs. mixed-language training to quantify cross-lingual transfer effects and demonstrate that multilingual training improves even Python performance through shared reasoning patterns.

title: SWE-smith-Multi: Scaling Cross-Language Software Engineering Training Data via Language-Agnostic Bug Synthesis
description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates impressive scaling for Python repositories, but real-world software engineering spans multiple languages (JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, Go, Rust). Current LM agents trained only on Python data exhibit significant performance degradation on non-Python codebases, limiting their practical utility. Proposed Method: We extend SWE-smith's pipeline to support polyglot bug synthesis by building language-agnostic execution environment templates (Docker-based) and test-breaking mutation operators for JavaScript/TypeScript (Jest/Mocha), Java (JUnit/Maven), Go (go test), and Rust (cargo test). We introduce a unified task instance schema that abstracts over language-specific tooling, enabling cross-language training. We further propose Cross-Language Curriculum Learning (CLCL), where models are first trained on high-volume Python instances, then progressively fine-tuned on sparser non-Python instances, using Python-derived reasoning patterns as transfer priors. Experiments: (1) Collect 10k+ instances per language from 50+ repositories each; (2) Train SWE-agent-LM variants with CLCL versus naive multilingual mixing; (3) Evaluate on SWE-bench Verified (Python), SWE-bench-JS (newly collected JavaScript benchmark), and existing Java/Go bug-fix benchmarks; (4) Ablate cross-language transfer quality by measuring zero-shot performance on unseen languages. We expect CLCL to outperform monolingual training by 8-15% on non-Python benchmarks.

title: SWE-smith for Multilingual Codebases: Scaling Software Engineering Training Data Beyond Python
description:

We handle language-specific challenges: JavaScript's dynamic typing requiring runtime-detectable mutations, Java's compilation step, and Rust's strict type system. Experiments: (1) Train language-specific SWE-agents and a unified multilingual agent on the new datasets; (2) Evaluate on SWE-bench analogues for each language (SWE-bench-JS, SWE-bench-Java); (3) Measure cross-lingual transfer: does training on Python+Java improve Java-only performance?; (4) Ablate mutation operator effectiveness per language; (5) Compare multilingual unified agent vs. ensemble of specialized agents on mixed-language repositories. We release all datasets, environments, and models openly.

title: SWE-smith for Low-Resource Languages: Scaling Software Engineering Training Data Beyond Python
description:
Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates scalable data generation for Python, but the software engineering community relies heavily on other languages (JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, Rust, Go) where LM-based agents lag significantly behind. Current multilingual SE benchmarks are tiny and manually curated, leaving non-Python agent training severely data-starved.

Proposed Method: We extend the SWE-smith pipeline to support JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, and Rust by (1) building language-specific execution environment constructors using Docker with appropriate runtimes and package managers (npm, Maven/Gradle, Cargo), (2) developing language-agnostic test-breaking mutation operators (statement deletion, type perturbation, API signature changes) adapted to each language's test frameworks (Jest, JUnit, cargo test), and (3) constructing automated environment validation to ensure reproducibility across 50+ repositories per language. We analyze whether cross-lingual transfer helps, whether Python-trained agents generalize, and measure data efficiency curves per language, producing actionable insights for multilingual SE agent development.

title: SWE-smith-Multi: Cross-Language Scaling of Software Engineering Training Data via Language-Agnostic Test-Breaking Synthesis
description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates impressive scaling for Python, but real-world software engineering spans multiple languages (JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, Go, Rust). We further train a lightweight 'environment router' that, given a repository, selects optimal mutation strategies per language to maximize valid task instance yield. Experiments: We generate 10k+ instances per language across 50+ repositories each. We fine-tune Qwen-2.5-32B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill models on combined multilingual datasets and evaluate on SWE-bench Verified (Python), GitBug-Java, and a newly curated SWE-bench-TS benchmark we construct. title: SWE-smith for Multilingual Codebases: Extending Automated Bug Synthesis Beyond Python to Java, TypeScript, and Rust
description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates scalable bug synthesis for Python, but real-world software engineering spans many languages. Experiments: We evaluate on (a) newly constructed held-out multilingual SWE-bench splits for each language, (b) cross-language transfer (train on Python+Java, test on TypeScript), and (c) ablations on dataset scale and mixing ratios. description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates impressive scaling for Python repositories, but real-world software engineering spans multiple languages (JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, Go, Rust). Experiments: We evaluate on SWE-bench Verified (Python), plus new held-out benchmarks we construct for JavaScript (SWE-bench-JS) and Java (SWE-bench-Java) using the same pipeline. We measure cross-language transfer, comparing joint training vs. language-specific training, and analyze whether Python-scale data bootstraps low-resource language performance.

title: SWE-multilang: Extending Scalable Bug Synthesis Beyond Python to Multi-Language Software Engineering Benchmarks
description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates scalable automated bug synthesis for Python, but the vast majority of real-world software engineering spans multiple languages (Java, TypeScript, Rust, Go, C++). LM agents trained solely on Python data exhibit poor cross-language transfer, and no equivalent large-scale training corpus exists for other languages.
