We curate a 100k+ instance dataset spanning 5 languages from 300+ GitHub repositories. Experiments: We train multilingual SWE-agents on this corpus and evaluate on (a) SWE-bench Verified (Python), (b) newly constructed SWE-bench-Java and SWE-bench-TypeScript benchmarks drawn from popular open-source repos, and (c) cross-language transfer experiments where models trained on one language are tested on another. We analyze whether shared training improves or hurts per-language performance and which fault injection strategies generalize across language families.

title: SWE-Diversity: Curriculum-Aware Difficulty Stratification for Software Engineering Training Data
description:
Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates that scale matters for SE agent training, but treats all 50k instances uniformly during training. Real software bugs vary enormously in difficulty—from single-line typos to multi-file architectural issues—and naive mixing may cause models to underfit hard instances or overfit trivial ones, limiting the ceiling of agent performance.

Method: We propose a difficulty stratification and curriculum learning framework for SE training data. First, we define a multi-dimensional difficulty score for each SWE-smith instance using proxy signals: number of files modified in the oracle patch, cyclomatic complexity of changed functions, test dependency depth, and semantic distance between bug-inducing change and existing tests. We cluster instances into difficulty tiers (Easy/Medium/Hard) and train agents using three curricula: (1) easy-to-hard progressive training, (2) hard-first training, and (3) stratified batch sampling ensuring balanced difficulty exposure. We also investigate whether hard instances benefit from synthetic chain-of-thought trajectory augmentation generated by a stronger teacher model.

Experiments: Train SWE-agent-LM-32B variants on each curriculum using the SWE-smith 50k dataset. Evaluate on SWE-bench Verified, stratified by difficulty tier. Measure Pass@1 overall and per-tier, training efficiency (performance vs. compute), and generalization to held-out repositories. We expect curriculum training to yield 3-5% absolute improvement on hard instances with no regression on easy ones.

title: SWE-Diversity: Curriculum-Guided Difficulty Stratification for Software Engineering Training Data
description:
Problem: SWE-smith generates 50k task instances at scale, but treats all instances as equally valuable during training. Software engineering tasks vary enormously in complexity—from single-line typo fixes to multi-file architectural refactors—and naive uniform sampling likely wastes compute on trivial instances while underrepresenting challenging ones that drive capability gains.

Proposed Method: We introduce an automated difficulty stratification pipeline for SWE-smith-generated instances. We define a multi-dimensional difficulty score combining: (1) static features (number of files modified, cyclomatic complexity delta, test interdependency depth), (2) dynamic features (agent rollout failure rate across a small LM probe, number of reasoning steps in successful trajectories), and (3) semantic novelty (embedding distance from training distribution). Using these scores, we construct a curriculum training procedure—Easy→Medium→Hard—and compare against competence-based self-paced learning and difficulty-weighted loss sampling. We additionally investigate 'hard negative mining': augmenting training with near-miss trajectories where the agent produced plausible but incorrect patches.

Experiments: Train SWE-agent-LM variants on stratified subsets (10k, 25k, 50k) using each curriculum strategy. Evaluate on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Lite, and a held-out hard-only split. Ablate difficulty dimensions to identify which signals matter most. Primary hypothesis: curriculum training on 25k stratified instances matches or exceeds uniform training on 50k, improving data efficiency by 2×.

title: SWE-Diversity: Quality-Aware Curriculum Sampling for Software Engineering Training Data
description:
Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates that scale matters for software engineering agents, but 50k instances sourced from 128 repositories may still suffer from distributional imbalance—easy bug patterns dominate, repositories with large test suites contribute disproportionately, and synthetic bugs may cluster around trivial mutations. Simply training on more data without considering difficulty or diversity may yield diminishing returns or even harm generalization to hard real-world issues.

Proposed Method: We introduce a quality-aware curriculum sampling framework that operates on top of SWE-smith-style datasets. First, we characterize each task instance along three axes: (1) structural complexity (AST edit distance, cyclomatic complexity of changed code), (2) test coverage entanglement (how many tests a fix must satisfy simultaneously), and (3) repository novelty (embedding-based distance from training distribution). We then train models using a dynamic curriculum that progressively emphasizes harder and more diverse instances, guided by per-instance learning signal (loss reduction per gradient step). We also introduce a de-duplication pass using fuzzy code-change fingerprints to remove near-duplicate synthetic bugs.

Experiments: We train 7B and 32B models on SWE-smith data under (a) uniform sampling, (b) difficulty-stratified curriculum, and (c) our full quality-aware curriculum. We evaluate on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Lite, and a held-out set of repositories unseen during training, measuring Pass@1, generalization gap, and data efficiency (performance vs. fraction of training data used).

title: SWE-smith-Multi: Extending Automated Software Engineering Data Synthesis to Polyglot Codebases
description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates impressive scalability for Python, but real-world software engineering increasingly involves multi-language codebases (TypeScript/JavaScript, Rust, Go, Java). Existing benchmarks like SWE-bench are Python-centric, leaving LM agents undertrained for polyglot environments where bugs span language boundaries (e.g., a Python backend calling a Rust extension, or a TypeScript frontend with a Go microservice). Proposed Method: We extend the SWE-smith pipeline to support four additional languages by (1) building language-specific execution environment constructors that handle heterogeneous build systems (cargo, npm, gradle, go modules), (2) developing cross-language test-breaking mutation operators that respect each language's type system and idioms, and (3) introducing inter-language task instances where the bug fix requires modifying files in two or more languages. We create a 30k-instance polyglot dataset from 200+ GitHub repositories spanning these languages. We then fine-tune a 32B base model on a combined Python+polyglot corpus and evaluate on both SWE-bench Verified and a newly constructed SWE-bench-Poly benchmark we release covering 200 real cross-language issues. Experiments compare: (a) language-specific vs. unified training, (b) transfer learning from Python-only pre-training, and (c) agent performance on mono- vs. cross-language bug fixes, measuring resolve rate and edit localization accuracy.

title: SWE-Diversity: Curriculum-Guided Difficulty Stratification for Software Engineering Training Data
description: Problem: SWE-smith generates large volumes of training instances but treats them as a flat, undifferentiated dataset. Training on uniformly sampled data ignores the varying difficulty, diversity, and pedagogical value of instances, potentially wasting compute on trivial examples or overwhelming models with premature hard cases. Method: We propose SWE-Diversity, a framework that automatically stratifies SWE-smith instances by difficulty and type, then applies curriculum learning during agent training. Difficulty estimation uses proxy signals: number of files/functions affected, cyclomatic complexity of changed code, test failure specificity, and a small 'oracle' model's pass rate. We cluster instances along axes of bug type (logic errors, missing branches, type mismatches, off-by-one), codebase domain (web, scientific, CLI), and fix length. We then train agents using three curricula: easy-to-hard, diversity-maximizing round-robin, and adaptive curriculum based on per-cluster rolling accuracy. Experiments: Starting from SWE-smith's 50k dataset, we train 7B and 32B base models under each curriculum and compare against uniform sampling on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Lite. We measure sample efficiency (performance vs. training instances seen), generalization to held-out repositories, and whether curriculum order improves robustness on hard instances. We expect 3-5% absolute improvement with 40% fewer training steps.

title: SWE-Diversity: Quality-Aware Curriculum Learning for Software Engineering Agents via Difficulty-Stratified Synthetic Data
description: Problem: While SWE-smith dramatically scales training data quantity, not all 50k instances are equally valuable for learning. Naively training on all instances ignores difficulty distribution, redundancy, and the curriculum effect—easy bugs may be unhelpful noise while extremely hard bugs may prevent learning. There is no principled approach to selecting and ordering synthetic SWE training data for maximum agent improvement. Method: We propose a quality-aware curriculum learning framework for SWE training data. First, we develop an automated difficulty estimator using code complexity metrics (cyclomatic complexity, call graph depth, number of files modified) combined with a small proxy model's solve probability to assign difficulty scores to each SWE-smith instance. Second, we apply coreset selection within difficulty strata to reduce redundancy while preserving coverage across repository types and bug categories. Third, we train agents using a curriculum scheduler that progressively introduces harder instances, with dynamic pacing based on the agent's rolling solve rate on a held-out validation split. Experiments: We compare (1) random sampling baselines, (2) difficulty-only filtering, (3) coreset-only selection, and (4) full curriculum training—all controlling for total training compute. Evaluation on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Lite measures whether curriculum ordering improves sample efficiency, generalization to unseen repositories, and performance on hard multi-file bugs specifically.

title: SWE-polyglot: Scaling Software Engineering Training Data Beyond Python via Cross-Language Environment Synthesis
description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates scalable training data generation for Python, but real-world software engineering spans JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, Go, Rust, and C++. Language models trained only on Python SWE tasks exhibit poor transfer to other languages, limiting deployment in polyglot codebases. Existing multilingual SE benchmarks (e.g., SWE-bench-Java) remain tiny (<500 instances), and no scalable pipeline exists for non-Python languages. Proposed Method: We extend the SWE-smith pipeline to support five additional languages by (1) designing language-agnostic environment containerization using standardized build manifests (npm, Maven, Gradle, Cargo, Go modules), (2) developing language-specific test-breaking mutation operators (type erasure mutations for TypeScript, borrow-checker violations for Rust, null-safety mutations for Java), and (3) creating a unified cross-language task schema enabling joint training. We synthesize ~10k instances per language (50k total) from 200+ repositories and train a single polyglot SWE-agent on the combined corpus. Experiments: (1) Zero-shot cross-language transfer vs. Python-only baseline on SWE-bench-Java and newly constructed SWE-bench-JS/Go benchmarks; (2) Ablation on joint vs. language-specific fine-tuning; (3) Analysis of mutation operator diversity vs. task solve rate; (4) Human evaluation of task realism across languages. We release all environments, datasets, and models publicly.

title: SWE-Critic: Learning a Reward Model for Software Engineering Agents via Contrastive Trajectory Labeling
description:
Problem: While SWE-smith provides large-scale task instances and solution trajectories, training data alone may be insufficient for teaching agents *when to trust their own patches*. Current SWE agents lack calibrated self-evaluation, leading to high false-positive submission rates and wasted compute on incorrect fixes.

Proposed Method: We leverage SWE-smith's 50k instances to construct a contrastive reward model (SWE-Critic) that scores agent-generated patches. For each task instance, we collect multiple trajectories (both passing and failing) using SWE-agent-LM-32B with temperature sampling. We create preference pairs: (passing trajectory, failing trajectory) and train a Bradley-Terry reward model on top of a code LM encoder. The reward model learns to distinguish subtle correctness signals—test alignment, localization accuracy, edit minimality—without requiring execution at inference time. We then use SWE-Critic as a reranker (Best-of-N) and as a process reward signal for RLVR fine-tuning.

Experiments: (1) Reranking evaluation on SWE-bench Verified/Lite comparing Pass@1 with N=4,8,16 samples; (2) RLVR fine-tuning loop using SWE-Critic as a verifier against execution-based ground truth; (3) Ablations on reward model architecture and preference pair construction strategies; (4) Generalization to non-Python repositories from SWE-bench Multilingual.

title: SWE-smith for Multilingual Codebases: Scaling Software Engineering Training Data Beyond Python
description: Problem: SWE-smith's pipeline is Python-specific, relying on Python execution environments and test frameworks (pytest). The majority of real-world software engineering happens in JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, Go, and Rust, yet no scalable task-instance generation pipeline exists for these languages, leaving non-Python SE agents severely data-starved. Proposed Method: We extend SWE-smith's core pipeline to support four additional languages by (1) building language-specific execution environment constructors using Docker with appropriate runtimes and package managers (npm/Maven/Go modules/Cargo), (2) adapting the fault-injection synthesis module to language-specific test frameworks (Jest, JUnit, go test, cargo test), and (3) introducing a cross-language difficulty calibration module that normalizes task complexity scores across languages using LM-judged oracle solutions. We generate ~10k instances per language (40k total) from 50+ repositories each, creating the first large-scale multilingual SWE benchmark dataset. Experiments: We fine-tune Qwen2.5-32B separately per language and in a unified multilingual model, evaluating on language-specific SWE-bench variants (SWE-bench-JS, newly constructed SWE-bench-Java). Ablations study transfer learning across languages, the value of multilingual joint training, and whether Python-trained agents zero-shot generalize to other languages. We release all pipelines, datasets, and models openly.

title: SWE-Diversity: Quality-Aware Curriculum Sampling for Software Engineering Training Data
description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates that scale matters for software engineering agents, but not all 50k instances are equally informative—some bugs are trivially simple (single-line edits), while others require deep multi-file reasoning. Naively training on all instances uniformly may waste compute on easy examples or overwhelm models with hard ones, limiting sample efficiency. Proposed Method: We introduce a quality-aware curriculum sampling framework that automatically characterizes task difficulty and diversity for SWE-smith instances along multiple axes: (1) patch complexity (lines changed, files touched, AST edit distance), (2) test structure (assertion depth, coverage delta), (3) error type taxonomy (logic, type, boundary, concurrency), and (4) repository domain clustering. We then train models using dynamic curriculum learning—starting with moderate-difficulty instances and gradually introducing harder ones—combined with diversity-aware sampling to ensure balanced coverage across error types and domains. A lightweight difficulty predictor is trained online using model confidence signals as proxy labels. Experiments: We train 7B and 32B base models on SWE-smith with (a) uniform sampling, (b) difficulty-only curriculum, (c) diversity-only sampling, and (d) our combined approach. Evaluation on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Lite, and held-out repositories measures resolve rate, sample efficiency (performance vs. training FLOPs), and generalization to unseen codebases. We expect 3-5% absolute improvement over uniform training with 40% fewer training steps.

title: SWE-polyglot: Extending Scalable Bug Synthesis and Agent Training Beyond Python to Multi-Language Software Repositories
description:
Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates scalable training data generation for Python, but the vast majority of real-world software engineering spans multiple languages (JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, Go, Rust, C/C++). Existing benchmarks and agents remain Python-centric, leaving a large portion of practical SE tasks unaddressed and limiting generalization of LM-based agents.

Proposed Method: We extend the SWE-smith pipeline to support multi-language repositories by (1) building language-agnostic execution environment constructors that handle package managers (npm, Maven, Cargo, Go modules) and test frameworks (Jest, JUnit, cargo test, go test), (2) designing language-aware fault injection strategies that exploit each language's type system and idioms to synthesize realistic breaking changes, and (3) constructing a unified 50k+ instance multi-language dataset (SWE-polyglot) spanning at least 5 languages across 200+ repositories.

We then fine-tune a 32B LM on SWE-polyglot and evaluate on both existing benchmarks (SWE-bench Verified for Python) and newly constructed held-out benchmarks for each supported language, measuring cross-language transfer and within-language resolve rates.

Experiments: (1) Ablations on monolingual vs. multilingual training mixtures, (2) zero-shot cross-language transfer from Python-only training, (3) scaling analysis of resolve rate vs. dataset size per language, (4) human study validating realism of synthesized multi-language bugs.

title: SWE-smith-Multi: Cross-Language Scaling of Software Engineering Training Data Beyond Python
description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates powerful scalable data generation for Python repositories, but real-world software engineering spans diverse languages (TypeScript, Java, Rust, Go). Models trained only on Python data exhibit poor cross-language transfer, limiting their utility for enterprise software engineering agents. Proposed Method: We extend the SWE-smith pipeline to support multi-language execution environments by (1) building language-specific containerization templates that handle package managers (npm, Maven, Cargo, Go modules), (2) developing language-agnostic test-breaking mutation operators that corrupt function signatures, introduce type mismatches, and delete logic branches across language ASTs, and (3) creating a unified cross-language trajectory format enabling joint training. We generate ~10k instances per language across TypeScript, Java, Rust, and Go repositories (40k total, ~128 repos per language), then train a unified multilingual SWE-agent on combined Python+multi-language data. title: SWE-Diversity: Quality-Aware Curriculum Sampling for Software Engineering Training Data
description: Problem: SWE-smith generates 50k training instances at scale, but treats all instances uniformly during training. In practice, instances vary dramatically in difficulty, code domain, bug type, and solution complexity. Naive uniform sampling may lead to suboptimal learning dynamics—easy instances waste compute while extremely hard instances cause unstable gradients. Proposed Method: We introduce a quality-aware curriculum learning framework for SWE-bench-style training data. First, we develop an automatic instance characterization pipeline that scores each SWE-smith instance along multiple axes: (1) difficulty estimated via a weak reference model's solve rate, (2) novelty measured by embedding-space diversity relative to already-seen instances, (3) bug taxonomy (logic error, type error, off-by-one, etc.) via static analysis. Second, we train a lightweight 'difficulty predictor' meta-model to dynamically estimate instance hardness during training. Third, we implement a curriculum scheduler that gradually shifts sampling from easier/diverse instances toward harder ones, with diversity-weighted deduplication to prevent mode collapse. Experiments: We train 7B and 32B models on SWE-smith's 50k instances using (a) uniform sampling, (b) difficulty-only curriculum, (c) our full diversity+difficulty curriculum. title: SWE-Critic: Training Reward Models for Software Engineering Agents via Automated Execution Feedback
description:
Problem: Current software engineering agents rely on supervised fine-tuning from expert trajectories, but lack reliable reward signals for reinforcement learning or best-of-N selection. Evaluating candidate patches requires running full test suites, which is expensive, while learned reward models could enable efficient online RL and inference-time scaling.

Proposed Method: Leveraging SWE-smith's large-scale dataset of 50k task instances with execution environments, we train a specialized reward model (SWE-Critic) that predicts patch correctness without executing tests. We generate diverse candidate patches per instance using multiple sampling temperatures from SWE-agent-LM-32B, label them via test execution (pass/fail), and train a discriminative reward model on (issue description, codebase context, candidate patch) → correctness probability. We explore contrastive training objectives comparing passing vs. failing patches and investigate whether the reward model generalizes to unseen repositories.

Experiments: (1) Reranking: use SWE-Critic to select among N=8/16/32 sampled patches, measuring Pass@1 improvement on SWE-bench Verified; (2) RL fine-tuning: use SWE-Critic as a proxy reward for PPO/GRPO training, comparing against execution-based RL; (3) Generalization: evaluate on repositories not seen during SWE-smith collection; (4) Ablations on training data size, context window, and architecture choices. Target: demonstrate >5% absolute improvement over greedy decoding via reranking alone.

title: SWE-Diversity: Quality-Aware Curriculum Learning for Software Engineering Agents via Difficulty-Stratified Synthetic Data
description:
Problem: SWE-smith generates large quantities of training instances but treats them uniformly during training, ignoring that instances vary enormously in difficulty, type (logic errors, API misuse, off-by-one bugs), and repository characteristics. Proposed Method: We introduce a quality-aware curriculum learning framework on top of SWE-smith data. Experiments: (1) Ablate curriculum schedules (random, easy-to-hard, hard-to-easy, adaptive) on SWE-bench Verified. (2) Compare difficulty-weighted vs. uniform training at 7B, 14B, 32B scales. (3) Analyze per-difficulty-tier resolution rates to measure if curriculum reduces the easy/hard performance gap. (4) Test generalization to SWE-bench Multilingual to assess cross-language transfer from Python-only training data.

title: SWE-polyglot: Extending Scalable Software Engineering Data Generation to Multi-Language Codebases
description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates scalable data generation for Python, but real-world software engineering spans many languages (Java, TypeScript, Rust, Go, C++). title: SWE-Diversity: Quality-Aware Curriculum Sampling for Software Engineering Training Data
description:

Using these signals, we train a data selection policy via a bandit-style algorithm that dynamically adjusts sampling probabilities during fine-tuning to maintain a target difficulty distribution, inspired by self-paced learning.

Experiments: We fine-tune Qwen-32B on SWE-smith instances using (a) uniform sampling, (b) difficulty-stratified curriculum, (c) novelty-weighted sampling, and (d) our adaptive policy. We ablate which quality axes matter most and show that 20k carefully selected instances outperform training on the full 50k.

title: SWE-polyglot: Extending Scalable Software Engineering Data Synthesis to Multi-Language Codebases

title: SWE-polyglot: Extending Scalable Software Engineering Data Synthesis Beyond Python to Multi-Language Codebases
description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates scalable synthesis of software engineering training data but is limited to Python codebases, leaving vast ecosystems (JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, Go, Rust) untapped. title: SWE-Critic: Learning a Reward Model for Software Engineering Agents from Synthetic Execution Feedback

title: SWE-polyglot: Extending Scalable Software Engineering Data Generation Beyond Python to Multi-Language Codebases
description:
Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates scalable training data generation for Python, but real-world software engineering spans many languages (JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, Go, Rust, C++). LM agents trained only on Python data struggle to generalize to polyglot repositories, limiting practical applicability. Current benchmarks and training pipelines are Python-centric, creating a significant capability gap.

Proposed Method: We extend the SWE-smith pipeline to support JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, and Go codebases. The key challenges are: (1) adapting execution environment construction to language-specific package managers (npm, Maven/Gradle, Go modules) and test frameworks (Jest, JUnit, Go test); (2) designing language-agnostic fault injection strategies that break existing tests (mutating type annotations, logic operators, API signatures); (3) creating unified trajectory collection across languages using language server protocol (LSP) tooling for consistent code navigation. We build a 30k-instance multilingual dataset from 200+ GitHub repositories across four languages.

Experiments: We fine-tune Qwen-2.5-32B on (a) Python-only, (b) single-language, and (c) mixed multilingual data, evaluating on SWE-bench Verified (Python), a newly constructed SWE-bench-JS benchmark (500 TypeScript/JavaScript issues), and existing Java/Go repair benchmarks. We measure cross-language transfer and whether multilingual training improves or degrades Python performance, analyzing data mixing ratios.

title: SWE-smith-Multi: Scaling Cross-Language Software Engineering Training Data Beyond Python
description:
Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates impressive scaling for Python repositories, but real-world software engineering spans multiple languages (JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, Go, Rust, C++). Models trained only on Python data show poor cross-language transfer for bug-fixing tasks, limiting their practical utility. Existing multilingual SE benchmarks (e.g., SWE-bench variants) remain Python-centric.

Proposed Method: We extend the SWE-smith pipeline to JavaScript/TypeScript (Node.js/Jest), Java (Maven/Gradle/JUnit), and Go ecosystems. The key technical contributions are: (1) language-agnostic execution environment construction using containerized build systems, (2) cross-language test breakage synthesis by adapting SWE-smith's mutation strategies (identifier renaming, logic inversion, boundary changes) to each language's AST via tree-sitter, and (3) a unified task instance format enabling joint multilingual training. We generate ~15k instances per language from 50+ repositories each, totaling ~100k cross-language instances.

Experiments: We train Qwen2.5-32B on (a) Python-only SWE-smith data, (b) multilingual data, and (c) combined datasets. Evaluation uses SWE-bench Verified (Python), GitBug-Java, and a newly curated JS/TS benchmark of 200 real GitHub issues. We measure cross-language transfer, per-language resolve rates, and ablate the impact of multilingual mixing ratios on Python performance to assess positive/negative transfer tradeoffs.

title: SWE-Diversity: Quality-Aware Data Curation for Software Engineering Agents via Difficulty Stratification and Repository Coverage Optimization
description: Problem: SWE-smith scales data quantity dramatically, but training on 50k instances naively may suffer from redundancy, uneven difficulty distribution, and repository-level biases that limit generalization. Simply scaling data volume does not guarantee proportional performance gains if the curriculum lacks diversity in bug complexity, code patterns, and repository characteristics. Proposed Method: We introduce SWE-Diversity, a data curation framework that operates on top of SWE-smith-generated instances to construct optimally diverse training sets. First, we embed task instances using code-aware representations (AST features + LM embeddings) and cluster them to identify redundant groups. Second, we estimate instance difficulty via proxy signals: number of files touched, test proximity to bug, cyclomatic complexity of modified functions, and agent solve-rate from lightweight sampling. Third, we construct training curricula using difficulty stratification (easy→hard scheduling) and coverage-maximizing subset selection via facility location optimization across repository types, bug categories, and difficulty tiers. We also introduce cross-repository generalization splits to measure out-of-distribution performance. Experiments: We train models on SWE-smith data versus SWE-Diversity-curated subsets of equal size (5k, 10k, 25k instances), evaluating on SWE-bench Verified and a new held-out repository benchmark. We measure whether 10k curated instances match 50k uncurated instances, and analyze which difficulty strata drive performance gains.

title: SWE-Diversity: Curriculum-Guided Difficulty-Aware Sampling for Software Engineering Training Data
description:
Problem: While SWE-smith dramatically scales training data volume, it treats all 50k instances uniformly during training. This ignores a critical dimension: task difficulty and structural diversity. Models trained on uniform distributions may plateau early, spending compute on trivially easy instances or failing to generalize across difficulty levels.

Proposed Method: We introduce a difficulty-aware curriculum learning framework for SWE-smith data. First, we develop an automated difficulty estimator using static code features (cyclomatic complexity, test dependency depth, edit distance of gold patch) and dynamic signals (agent rollout success rates across multiple LM sizes). We then cluster instances along difficulty and structural axes (single-file vs. multi-file edits, bug type taxonomy via AST analysis). Training proceeds via a curriculum scheduler that progressively introduces harder instances, with importance sampling to maintain diversity across repository types and bug categories. We also apply data pruning to remove near-duplicate instances using embedding-based deduplication of task descriptions and patches.

Experiments: (1) Compare flat vs. curriculum training on SWE-bench Verified using 7B and 32B base models; (2) Ablate difficulty signal sources; (3) Evaluate generalization to SWE-bench Multilingual and out-of-distribution repositories; (4) Analyze sample efficiency—achieving equivalent performance with 50% fewer training instances. We expect 3-5% absolute improvement in resolve rate and 2x faster convergence.

title: SWE-smith for Multilingual Codebases: Scaling Software Engineering Training Data Beyond Python
description:
Problem: SWE-smith and existing SWE-bench benchmarks focus exclusively on Python, yet real-world software engineering spans diverse languages (TypeScript, Java, Rust, Go). LMs trained only on Python bug-fix trajectories may develop language-specific reasoning patterns that fail to generalize, leaving a critical gap for multilingual software engineering agents.

Proposed Method: We extend the SWE-smith pipeline to support non-Python repositories by (1) building language-agnostic execution environment constructors using Docker with per-language test harnesses (Jest, JUnit, Cargo test, go test), (2) developing language-specific fault injection strategies that break existing tests by mutating syntax/semantics appropriate to each language's type system, and (3) generating 10k+ task instances each for TypeScript, Java, Rust, and Go from 50+ popular GitHub repositories per language. We then train multilingual SWE-agents using cross-lingual mixture training and study whether joint training across languages improves or hurts per-language performance.

Experiments: (1) Benchmark newly created multilingual task instances with existing frontier models to establish baselines; (2) compare monolingual vs. multilingual fine-tuned agents on per-language resolve rates; (3) ablate training data mixtures to find optimal cross-lingual ratios; (4) evaluate zero-shot transfer—train on Python+Java, test on Rust—to measure cross-language generalization of bug-fixing capabilities.

title: SWE-smith-Multi: Scaling Cross-Language Software Engineering Training Data via Unified Execution Environments
description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates impressive scalability for Python codebases, but real-world software engineering increasingly involves polyglot repositories (TypeScript, Rust, Java, Go) and cross-language bugs. Current benchmarks and training pipelines remain Python-centric, leaving a significant gap in agent capabilities for non-Python ecosystems. Method: We extend SWE-smith's pipeline to support four additional languages (TypeScript/JavaScript, Rust, Java, Go) by designing language-agnostic execution environment templates using containerized build systems (Docker + Nix), unified test-failure detection interfaces, and language-specific fault injection operators (e.g., type erasure for TypeScript, lifetime violations for Rust, null-safety breaks for Java). We introduce a cross-language instance generator that breaks existing tests by applying targeted AST-level mutations calibrated per language, then synthesizes 10k-30k instances per language from 50+ popular GitHub repositories each. We additionally create mixed-language task instances where bugs span FFI boundaries or configuration files. Experiments: We train 7B and 32B base models on combined multilingual datasets and evaluate on SWE-bench Verified (Python), a new SWE-bench-TS benchmark (TypeScript, 300 verified instances we curate), and existing Java/Rust repair benchmarks. Ablations measure the benefit of cross-language transfer, per-language data volume, and polyglot vs. monolingual training.

title: SWE-Diversity: Quality-Aware Curriculum Learning for Software Engineering Agents via Difficulty-Stratified Training Data
description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates that scaling training data quantity dramatically improves SE agent performance, but it remains unclear whether all 50k instances contribute equally—some may be trivially easy, redundant, or misleading noise that wastes compute and potentially harms generalization. Naively training on all instances treats a one-line typo fix identically to a complex multi-file refactoring. Proposed Method: We introduce a difficulty-aware curriculum pipeline that (1) automatically stratifies SWE-smith instances by estimated complexity using proxy signals (edit distance, number of files changed, cyclomatic complexity delta, test coverage change, reasoning chain length in trajectories), (2) trains a lightweight difficulty predictor to score new instances, (3) applies curriculum learning that progressively introduces harder instances during fine-tuning, and (4) performs influence-function-based data pruning to remove redundant or harmful instances. We also explore diversity-maximizing subset selection using embedding-space coverage metrics over code changes. Experiments: We fine-tune Qwen2.5-32B on difficulty-stratified subsets (10k, 25k, 50k) versus random baselines, evaluating on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Lite. We measure sample efficiency (performance per training instance), generalization to held-out repositories, and ablate curriculum ordering strategies. We hypothesize that 15k carefully curated instances can match or exceed training on all 50k, reducing compute by 3x.

title: SWE-smith for Multilingual Codebases: Scaling Software Engineering Training Data Beyond Python
description: Problem: SWE-smith demonstrates powerful scalable data generation for Python, but the vast majority of real-world software engineering happens across diverse languages (JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, Go, Rust, C++). LM-based agents trained only on Python data exhibit poor cross-language generalization, yet no scalable pipeline exists for generating execution-grounded bug-fix training data in non-Python languages. Proposed Method: We extend SWE-smith's pipeline to support multilingual codebases by: (1) building language-specific execution environment constructors using Docker with appropriate runtime toolchains (Node.js, JVM, Go toolchain, Cargo, CMake); (2) adapting the fault-seeding strategies (statement deletion, mutation operators, API misuse injection) to each language's AST via tree-sitter; (3) developing language-agnostic test-failure verification using standardized exit codes and structured test reporters (Jest, JUnit, go test, cargo test). We construct a 30k+ instance multilingual dataset spanning 5 languages from 200+ GitHub repositories. Experiments: (1) Train language-specific and unified multilingual SWE-agents on this data; (2) Evaluate on SWE-bench Verified (Python) plus new held-out benchmarks for each language; (3) Ablate cross-language transfer—does joint multilingual training improve Python performance and vice versa; (4) Compare fault-seeding mutation rates and diversity across languages to understand data quality differences.
